opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, fewer than people think. That's one of the most counterintuitive things I've learned doing this work. People imagine you need millions of people marching in the streets before anything changes, and sure, that would be nice, but that's not actually how most policy change happens.

If you look at historical advocacy movements, it's usually a surprisingly small number of dedicated, competent people who do the bulk of the work. A few dozen really committed people who show up, who write to their representatives, who talk to journalists, who brief policymakers, who are willing to have the awkward conversations, can move things a remarkable amount. Most politicians have never had a single constituent talk to them seriously about extinction risk from AI. So when even a handful of people do, that's a signal. They notice.

What we've found at Control AI is that when you actually go and talk to lawmakers and explain the situation plainly, that the people building these systems are themselves saying there's a real chance this kills everyone, and that nobody knows how to control superintelligence, a lot of them are genuinely receptive. They just didn't know. Nobody had told them. The bottleneck isn't that the argument is unconvincing. The bottleneck is that nobody's making it to the right people.

So I'd say the difference between zero and a hundred serious people is enormous. The difference between a hundred and a thousand is also big. After that you get into the territory of a broader public movement, which matters too, but you don't need to wait for that to start having an impact. The thing I always tell people is: don't assume someone else is handling it. Mostly, nobody is. If you care about this, your contribution is not a drop in the ocean. It might be one of very few drops there are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a few dozen committed people can matter and highlights the difference between zero, a hundred, and a thousand. It does not estimate that roughly 10,000 to 1 million people might suffice.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes Control AI speaking with lawmakers, but does not propose scaling advocacy through many independently operating groups modeled on Control AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that many. That's the thing people get wrong about this. They look at the problem and they think, well, this is a civilizational-scale issue, so surely you need a civilizational-scale movement, you need millions of people in the streets. And look, that would be great, I'd take it. But that's not how most political change actually happens. Most political change happens because a surprisingly small number of people showed up, were persistent, and were pointing at the right thing at the right time.

When we started Control AI, the thing that shocked me was how empty the room was. You'd go to Westminster, you'd go to Brussels, and you'd expect there to be, I don't know, armies of lobbyists and advocates already working on this. And there basically weren't. There were plenty of people lobbying for the labs, for sure, and there were people working on narrow issues like deepfakes or bias, which are real issues, but on the core question of "should we be building things smarter than us that we can't control," there was nobody. The seats were empty. So you'd walk into an MP's office, explain the situation in plain language, and they'd go, "wait, why has nobody told me this?" And that's a sign that the marginal person matters enormously.

The numbers I'd throw out, and these are rough, are something like: a dozen people doing this full time, seriously, in a given country, can move the Overton window noticeably. A few hundred people doing it part time, writing to their representatives, showing up to meetings, talking to journalists, can make it a live political issue. You don't need a majority of the population to understand transformer architectures. You need enough people to make it clear to politicians that this is something their constituents care about and that there's no political cost to taking it seriously, and ideally a cost to ignoring it.

Now, the caveat is that these people have to be effective. Numbers aren't the bottleneck, competence and persistence are. A lot of people in this space, and I say this with love, have spent years writing very long blog posts for each other instead of talking to anyone with actual power. That doesn't count. What counts is being willing to say, in normal human language, "this is dangerous, here's why, here's what we want you to do," and then say it again, and again, to the people who can actually do something. Most people won't do that because it feels uncomfortable or low status or like you're being too political. The ones who will do it are worth a hundred who won't.

So my honest answer is: fewer than you'd think, which means the person listening to this could be one of them, and that's not a motivational-poster thing, it's just how thin the field actually is.

r001.rationale: The response estimates roughly a dozen full-time advocates or a few hundred part-time advocates; it does not estimate 10,000 to 1 million people and instead says fewer are needed.

r002.rationale: It describes Control AI’s work but does not propose scaling advocacy through many independently operating groups modeled on Control AI.

astra-6.text: I don’t think there’s a magic number. A relatively small group of committed people can make a difference if they’re organized and have a clear demand. The question is less, “How many people agree with us?” and more, “How many people are actually doing something?” Are they talking to their representatives, organizing locally, explaining the issue to people around them? You need people who show up consistently. That gives other people something to join, and that’s how you build a larger movement.

r001.rationale: The response gives no estimate in the 10,000 to 1 million range; it only says a relatively small group can make a difference.

r002.rationale: It describes consistent organizing and building a larger movement, but does not propose many independently operating groups modeled on Control AI.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think there’s a magic number. A relatively small group of committed people can make a real difference if they’re organized and focused on a concrete political objective. You need people who can explain the issue clearly, build relationships, and keep showing up. It’s not just about getting a million people to sign a petition; it’s about turning concern into sustained political pressure. And different people can contribute different things—time, expertise, funding, or simply talking to their representatives. You don’t have to be a machine learning researcher to have a say in whether this technology is developed safely.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no magic number and that a relatively small group can help, but gives no estimate in the range of 10,000 to 1 million.

r002.rationale: It discusses organizing and varied contributions, but does not propose scaling advocacy through many independent groups modeled on Control AI.
